decisions.quote:
Salmela and Laurinen (2009) took an important step in the direction sug-
     gested by Kingdom (2011). hey generated versions of simultaneous bright-
     ness contrast, White’s illusion (White, 1979, see Figure 6) and the Benary
     cross (Benary, 1924), and masked them with narrowband noise. hen they
     measured the efect of the noise’s spatial frequency and orientation on per-
     ceived brightness. hey found that noise with a narrow frequency band (be-
     tween 1 and 5 cpd) had a strong masking efect on the illusions, meaning that
     the apparent brightness diferences were considerably reduced, whereas noise
     at higher or lower frequencies had little efect (see Figure 7). hey concluded
     that their results rsuggest that ilters below 1 cpd and above 5 cpd are not used
     in the computation of surface brightnesss.
        We replicated and extended Salmela and Laurinen’s (2009) results, and
     tested a number of diferent multi-scale spatial iltering models with respect to
     their capability to reproduce the psychophysically observed efects of narrow-
     band noise on lightness perception.
decisions.location: Part II, Introduction, p. 50, lines 49-63 (and References, p. 161, lines 3236-3238)
decisions.reason: The shipped row misidentified White (1979) as the replicated target from the abstract phrase 'Choosing White's illusion (White, 1979) as a test case, we replicated and extended the psychophysical results'. In the primary text, White (1979) is cited solely to name the classical stimulus phenomenon ('White’s illusion (White, 1979, see Figure 6)'), whereas the actual study whose psychophysical lightness-matching experiment and narrowband noise-masking findings are replicated and extended is Salmela and Laurinen (2009), matching blind target 0.

decisions.quote:
We replicated the main indings of Salmela
and Laurinen (2009). herefore a strong test of lightness models is testing
their predictions of results in the noise masking experiments. Speciically, the
models should predict (A) a reduction in illusion strength for noise frequen-
cies between 1 and 5 cpd, and (B) the location of this reduction along the fre-
quency axis should not shift proportionally with changes in grating frequency.
We tested these predictions by simulating our noise masking experiment with
the four models.
decisions.location: Part II, Section 6 (Effects of Noise on Perceived Lightness), p. 61, lines 352-359
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly state the overall replication verdict that they replicated the main psychophysical findings of Salmela and Laurinen (2009), observing the strongest masking effect for narrowband noise between 1 and 5 cpd without proportional scaling to grating frequency (also reiterated in Results lines 511-515 and Discussion lines 1010-1014). The shipped coding of 'failed' confused the new model-simulation extension—in which four multi-scale spatial filtering models failed to account for the replicated human psychophysical effect—with a failure of the replication itself.

decisions.quote:
We replicated and extended Salmela and Laurinen’s (2009) results, and
     tested a number of diferent multi-scale spatial iltering models with respect to
     their capability to reproduce the psychophysically observed efects of narrow-
     band noise on lightness perception.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding agree on 'replication'. The authors collected new psychophysical lightness-matching data from 11 observers (Section 7, lines 365-474) to re-test Salmela and Laurinen's (2009) narrowband noise-masking findings on White's illusion.

raw_expert_opinion.reason: The primary study conducts a psychophysical lightness-matching replication experiment with 11 human observers (Section 6, pp. 60-61; Section 7, pp. 62-72) testing the effect of narrowband spatial-frequency noise masking (0.58 to 9 cpd) on perceived lightness in White's illusion across three grating frequencies (0.4, 0.8, 1.6 cpd), directly retesting and comparing against Salmela and Laurinen's (2009) empirical finding that narrowband noise between 1 and 5 cpd strongly masks the illusion. The reference list (p. 161, lines 3236-3238) explicitly identifies 'Salmela, V. R., & Laurinen, P. I. (2009). Low-level features determine brightness in White’s and Benary’s illusions. Vision Research, 49(7), 682–90. doi: 10.1016/j.visres.2009.01.006', matching Crossref metadata. The only shipped candidate, row 2370 (10.1068/p080413; M. White, 1979, 'A New Effect of Pattern on Perceived Lightness', Perception 8(4):413-416), is the classic 1979 stimulus paper that introduced White's illusion, not a report of the 2009 narrowband noise-masking experiment. Report equivalence does not apply because they are independent studies published 30 years apart by different authors on different empirical questions. No prior adjudication or state files exist.
